What is printed by:
SET i = 1
WHILE i <= 3
  PRINT i
  SET i = i + 1
ENDWHILE
exp: i starts at 1. Check 1 <= 3 (true), print 1, i = 2. Check 2 <= 3 (true), print 2, i = 3. Check 3 <= 3 (true), print 3, i = 4. Check 4 <= 3 (false), loop ends. Printed output is 1 2 3. The answer is 1 2 3.

questions.q:
What is printed? (digit sum)
SET n = 123
SET s = 0
WHILE n > 0
  SET s = s + (n MOD 10)
  SET n = n DIV 10
ENDWHILE
PRINT s
exp: Each pass peels the last digit: n = 123 → s = 0+3 = 3, n = 12; s = 3+2 = 5, n = 1; s = 5+1 = 6, n = 0. The digits are 1, 2, 3 and their sum is 6. The answer is 6.

questions.q:
What is returned? (Capgemini-style GCD)
FUNCTION solve(p, q)
  WHILE q <> 0
    SET v = p MOD q
    SET p = q
    SET q = v
  ENDWHILE
  RETURN p
ENDFUNCTION
CALL solve(4, 2)
exp: This is the Euclidean GCD algorithm. p = 4, q = 2: v = 4 MOD 2 = 0, p = 2, q = 0. The check q <> 0 fails immediately and p = 2 is returned, the GCD of 4 and 2. The answer is 2.

questions.q:
What does this loop print?
SET i = 10
WHILE i < 5
  PRINT i
  SET i = i + 1
ENDWHILE
exp: The condition is checked first: is 10 < 5? No. Because a WHILE loop is condition-first, the body never runs even once, so nothing is printed. The answer is nothing.

questions.q: In a REPEAT-UNTIL loop, what is the MINIMUM number of times the body can execute?
exp: The UNTIL test sits below the body.
Control enters the body before any test is made.
So one pass always happens — zero is impossible.

questions.q:
Integer i
Set i = 3
REPEAT
  PRINT i + 3
  i = i - 1
UNTIL i = 0
What is the output?
exp: Pass 1 prints 3+3 = 6, i becomes 2.
Pass 2 prints 5, i becomes 1. Pass 3 prints 4, i becomes 0.
Equality test now TRUE -> exit. Output 6 5 4.

questions.q: For REPEAT v = v + s UNTIL v >= T with start a (a < T, s > 0), the number of passes is:
exp: Need smallest k with a + k*s >= T.
Solve: k >= (T-a)/s -> ceiling.

questions.q: C's do-while continues while its condition is TRUE. A Pascal-style REPEAT-UNTIL stops when its condition becomes ___.

do-while(C) = REPEAT UNTIL(NOT C).

problem.title: Large-Small Sum
problem.statement: Given an array, take elements at even indices (0, 2, 4...) and elements at odd indices (1, 3, 5...) separately. Find the second largest among even-index elements and the second smallest among odd-index elements, then print their sum. For example array 3 2 1 7 5 4 gives even part 3 1 5 with second largest 3 and odd part 2 7 4 with second smallest 4, so answer is 7. If either part has less than 2 elements print 0.
problem.inputFormat:
Line 1: n (size of array)
Line 2: n space-separated integers
problem.outputFormat: Print one integer which is the required sum, or 0 if not possible.
problem.starter:
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
# TODO: find second largest at even indices and second smallest at odd indices and print sum
problem.solution:
import sys
def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().strip().split()
    if not data:
        return
    n = int(data[0])
    arr = list(map(int, data[1:1+n]))
    even = [arr[i] for i in range(n) if i % 2 == 0]
    odd = [arr[i] for i in range(n) if i % 2 == 1]
    if len(even) < 2 or len(odd) < 2:
        print(0)
        return
    even_sorted = sorted(even)
    odd_sorted = sorted(odd)
    print(even_sorted[-2] + odd_sorted[1])
if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
problem.approach: Split the array by index parity, sort each part, then pick second largest from even part and second smallest from odd part.
steps: Make one list of items at even indices 0, 2, 4.
Make one list of items at odd indices 1, 3, 5.
If either list has less than 2 items print 0.
Sort both lists in increasing order.
Take second last of even list and second of odd list.
problem.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
problem.insight: Splitting by index parity turns it into two small sorting problems.

problem.title: AXIS Archetype: Customer Orders With Product Names
problem.statement: Tables Customers(customer_id, name), Orders(order_id, customer_id, product_id, qty), Products(product_id, product_name, price). Show customer name, product_name, qty, and line total (qty*price) as total for every order, ordered by order_id.
problem.schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Customers(customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Orders(order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, product_id INTEGER, qty INTEGER); CREATE TABLE Products(product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT, price INTEGER);
problem.seedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ravi'); INSERT INTO Products VALUES (10,'Pen',100),(20,'Book',250); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (100,1,10,2),(101,2,20,1),(102,1,20,3);
problem.hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (5,'K'),(6,'L'); INSERT INTO Products VALUES (50,'Desk',1000),(60,'Lamp',500); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (200,5,50,1),(201,6,60,4);
problem.solution: SELECT c.name, p.product_name, o.qty, (o.qty * p.price) AS total FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN Products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY o.order_id;
problem.starter:
-- customer, product, qty, total per order
SELECT c.name, p.product_name, o.qty, (o.qty * p.price) AS total
FROM Orders o
JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN Products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
problem.approach: Chain two JOINs from the fact table (Orders) to each dimension. Compute qty*price inline.
steps: Orders is the centre: one FK to Customers, one to Products.
First JOIN attaches customer names; second attaches product names+prices.
qty*price AS total computes the line value per row (no GROUP BY needed).
ORDER BY o.order_id keeps judge order deterministic.
problem.insight: This 3-table chain IS the AXIS SQL coding slot. Centre fact + two dimension JOINs.
problem.learn: Chain JOINs: fact table JOIN dim1 ON fk1 JOIN dim2 ON fk2.
